claim: The Frank-Starling relation ensures the volume of blood ejected in each heartbeat is matched to the extent of venous filling.
source: The Frank-Starling relation is a fundamental auto-regulatory property of the heart that ensures the volume of blood ejected in each heartbeat is matched to the extent of venous filling.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the Frank-Starling relation in the abstract.

claim: Heart muscle cells generate higher force when stretched.
source: At the cellular level, heart muscle cells generate higher force when stretched, but despite intense efforts the underlying molecular mechanism remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The underlying molecular mechanism for length-dependent activation in heart muscle remains unknown.
source: At the cellular level, heart muscle cells generate higher force when stretched, but despite intense efforts the underlying molecular mechanism remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: The enhanced force observed when heart muscle cells are maximally activated by calcium is due to a change in thick filament structure.
source: Our results show that the enhanced force observed when heart muscle cells are maximally activated by calcium is due to a change in thick filament structure, but the increase in calcium sensitivity at lower calcium levels is due to a change in thin filament structure.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The increase in calcium sensitivity at lower calcium levels is due to a change in thin filament structure.
source: Our results show that the enhanced force observed when heart muscle cells are maximally activated by calcium is due to a change in thick filament structure, but the increase in calcium sensitivity at lower calcium levels is due to a change in thin filament structure.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Increasing cardiac sarcomere length results in enhanced performance of cardiac muscle cells during the subsequent contraction.
source: At the cellular level, the Frank-Starling relationship implies that increasing cardiac sarcomere length results in enhanced performance of cardiac muscle cells during the subsequent contraction (Allen and Kentish, 1985; de Tombe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Myofilament length-dependent activation involves increases in maximum force developed by the myofilaments at high Ca2+ and increases in their sensitivity to Ca2+.
source: This myofilament length-dependent activation (LDA) is two-fold: with an increase in sarcomere length (SL), there are increases in (1) the maximum force developed by the myofilaments at high Ca2+ and (2) their sensitivity to Ca2+.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about LDA.

claim: Impaired LDA may contribute to the pathogenesis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and heart failure.
source: Impaired LDA and hence a defective Frank–Starling relationship may also contribute to the pathogenesis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and heart failure (Schwinger et al., 1994; Sequeira et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The detailed molecular mechanism for LDA in heart muscle remains elusive.
source: Although the Frank-Starling law of the heart is one of its fundamental properties and has been investigated for over a century, the detailed molecular mechanism for the LDA in heart muscle remains elusive.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Contraction of cardiac muscle is driven by an interaction between myosin and actin that is controlled by the transient binding of Ca2+ ions to troponin in the actin-containing thin filament.
source: Contraction of cardiac muscle is driven by an interaction between myosin and actin that is controlled by the transient binding of Ca2+ ions to troponin in the actin-containing thin filament on a beat-to-beat basis (Tobacman, 1996; Gordon et al., 2000; Kobayashi and Solaro, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: An increase in sarcomere length leads to a decreased inter-filament spacing.
source: An increase in SL leads to a decreased inter-filament spacing (Irving et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2013) and it has been suggested that this leads directly to an increase in Ca2+ sensitivity of force generation (McDonald and Moss, 1995; Fuchs and Smith, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The reduction of inter-filament spacing is unlikely to mediate LDA.
source: However, when osmotic compression of inter-filament spacing matches that induced by SL, the myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity is only affected by SL (Konhilas et al., 2002), indicating that the reduction of inter-filament spacing is unlikely to mediate LDA.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited experimental results.

claim: Titin-based passive tension in heart muscle cells seems to play an important role in LDA.
source: Titin-based passive tension in the heart muscle cells seems to play an important role in LDA (Cazorla et al., 2001; Fukuda et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A single titin molecule runs from the Z-disc to the M-line in the A-band contributing to muscle assembly and passive tension.
source: A single titin molecule runs from the Z-disc to the M-line in the A-band contributing to muscle assembly and passive tension (Labeit and Kolmerer, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Titin is largely responsible for the length-dependent passive tension of cardiac muscle.
source: The fact that titin is largely responsible for the length-dependent passive tension of cardiac muscle and also possesses both actin and myosin binding domains (Linke et al., 2002; Granzier and Labeit, 2004), makes it a candidate for the link between SL and force generating apparatus.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Titin possesses both actin and myosin binding domains.
source: The fact that titin is largely responsible for the length-dependent passive tension of cardiac muscle and also possesses both actin and myosin binding domains (Linke et al., 2002; Granzier and Labeit, 2004), makes it a candidate for the link between SL and force generating apparatus.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Length-dependent changes in the myosin head orientation in diastole may be a factor in LDA.
source: Small-angle X-ray diffraction studies suggest that length-dependent changes in the myosin head orientation in diastole may be a factor in LDA (Farman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Length-dependent structural changes are observed in the thin filament in diastole.
source: Moreover, a recent X-ray study shows that length-dependent structural changes are also observed in the thin filament in diastole (Ait-Mou et al., 2016), supporting the notion that thin filament activation may also play an important role in LDA.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The length-dependent changes in the structure of both thick and thin filaments are related to the titin strain.
source: The length-dependent changes in the structure of both thick and thin filaments are related to the titin strain (Ait-Mou et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Maximum active force at pCa 4.5 increased by ~40% when SL was increased from 1.9 to 2.3 μm.
source: Maximum active force at pCa 4.5 increased by ~40% when SL was increased from 1.9 to 2.3 μm (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Passive force increased in the same SL range by ~30% of maximum Ca2+-activated force at SL 1.9 μm.
source: Passive force increased in the same SL range by ~30% of maximum Ca2+-activated force at SL 1.9 μm (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Increasing SL produced a leftward shift of the Ca2+-force relationships, indicating an increase in myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity.
source: Increasing SL also produced a leftward shift of the Ca2+-force relationships, indicating an increase in myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The length-dependent changes in force are consistent with previous reports.
source: These length-dependent changes in force are consistent with previous reports (Kentish et al., 1986; Dobesh et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Ca2+ binding to the regulatory domain of troponin triggers a cascade of structural changes in the thin filament that lead to an azimuthal movement of tropomyosin around the filament.
source: Contraction of heart muscle is initiated by Ca2+ binding to the regulatory domain of troponin in the actin-containing thin filaments, that triggers a cascade of structural changes in the thin filament and leads to an azimuthal movement of tropomyosin around the filament that allow myosin to interact with actin and generate force (Tobacman, 1996; Gordon et al., 2000; Kobayashi and Solaro, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The IT arm of troponin anchors the troponin complex to the thin filament.
source: The IT arm of troponin, a rigid domain containing the C-terminal lobe of TnC and a coiled-coil formed by α-helices from troponin I (TnI) and troponin T (TnT), anchors the troponin complex to the thin filament.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about troponin structure.

claim: At a short SL of 1.9 μm, <P2> for BR-cTnC-C decreased by an average of −0.081 ± 0.005 between pCa 6 and 4.5.
source: At a short SL of 1.9 μm, with the increase of active force, <P2> for BR-cTnC-C decreased by an average of −0.081 ± 0.005 between pCa 6 and 4.5, the range of [Ca2+] where active force was developed (Figure 2c, Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Figure 2c and Table 1.

claim: The pCa50 for <P2> of BR-cTnC-C was 5.37 ± 0.02, almost identical to that for force in the same trabeculae.
source: The pCa50 for <P2> was 5.37 ± 0.02, almost identical to that for force in the same trabeculae (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Table 1.

claim: When trabeculae were stretched from SL 1.9 to 2.3 μm, the maximal Ca2+-activated force from trabeculae containing BR-cTnC-C increased by about 40%.
source: When trabeculae were stretched from SL 1.9 to 2.3 μm, the maximal Ca2+-activated force from trabeculae containing BR-cTnC-C increased by about 40% (Figure 2a and 3a, Table 1)
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Figures 2a, 3a, and Table 1.

claim: The pCa50 for force increased by 0.12 ± 0.01 (n = 5) pCa units when SL was increased from 1.9 to 2.3 μm.
source: and the pCa50 increased by 0.12 ± 0.01 (n = 5) pCa units, indicating an increase in Ca2+-sensitivity of force generation.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results.

claim: The pCa50 for <P2> of the BR-cTnC-C probe increased by 0.11 ± 0.02 pCa units when SL was increased from 1.9 to 2.3 μm.
source: The pCa50 for <P2> of the BR-cTnC-C probe also increased by 0.11 ± 0.02 pCa units, similar to that for force.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results.

claim: The amplitude of the change in <P2> (Δ<P2>) for BR-cTnC-C between pCa 6 and 4.5 was unaffected by SL increase.
source: In contrast with the effect on maximum Ca2+-activated force, the amplitude of the change in <P2> (Δ<P2> in Table 1) for BR-cTnC-C between pCa 6 and 4.5 was unaffected by SL increase (Figure 2c and 3c, Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Figures 2c, 3c, and Table 1.

claim: The steepness of the Ca2+-dependent changes for <P2> (nH) did not change significantly when the SL was increased.
source: The steepness of the Ca2+-dependent changes for <P2>, nH, also did not change significantly when the SL was increased (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Table 1.

claim: pCa50 for <P2> of the cTnC E helix probe at 1.9 μm SL was 5.34 ± 0.02, not significantly different from pCa50 for force in the same group of trabeculae.
source: pCa50 for <P2> of the cTnC E helix probe at 1.9 μm SL was 5.34 ± 0.02, not significantly different from pCa50 for force in the same group of trabeculae (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Table 1.

claim: Increasing SL from 1.9 to 2.3 μm significantly increased pCa50 for <P2> and force by 0.11 and 0.12 pCa units, respectively, for the E helix probe.
source: Increasing SL from 1.9 to 2.3 μm significantly increased pCa50 for <P2> and force by 0.11 and 0.12 pCa units, respectively, the same as for the C helix probe.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results.

claim: The changes in <P2> for the E helix probe during Ca2+-activation (Δ<P2>) were not affected by increasing SL from 1.9 to 2.3 μm.
source: Similar to that for BR-cTnC-C, the changes in <P2> for the C helix probe during Ca2+-activation (Δ<P2>) were not affected by increasing SL from 1.9 to 2.3 μm (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Table 1.

claim: For both the C and E helix probes, <P2> decreased upon Ca2+-activation and the overall changes in <P2> (Δ<P2>) were not affected by increasing SL from 1.9 to 2.3 μm while the maximal force generation was markedly enhanced.
source: For both the C and E helix probes, <P2> decreased upon Ca2+-activation and the overall changes in <P2> (Δ<P2>) were not affected by increasing SL from 1.9 to 2.3 μm while the maximal force generation was markedly enhanced (Figure 2 and 3 and Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Figures 2, 3, and Table 1.

claim: Increasing SL increased <P2> during both relaxation and active contraction, particularly for the BR-cTnC-E.
source: By contrast, increasing SL increased <P2> during both relaxation and active contraction, particularly for the BR-cTnC-E, i.e. the orientation change was in the opposite direction to that during Ca2+-activation (Figure 2d and Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Figure 2d and Table 1.

claim: The activation of the thin filament at maximum [Ca2+] (pCa 4.5) was not changed by increasing SL.
source: These two observations together suggested that the activation of the thin filament at maximum [Ca2+] (pCa 4.5) was not changed by increasing SL.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The increased <P2> at longer SL at all [Ca2+] may be related to the fact that ventricular trabeculae are made up of short branched cardiac muscle cells in which the myofibrils are not perfectly parallel.
source: The increased <P2> at longer SL at all [Ca2+] may be related to the fact that ventricular trabeculae are made up of short branched cardiac muscle cells in which the myofibrils are not perfectly parallel.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: The myofibrils are likely to become better aligned when trabeculae are stretched.
source: The myofibrils are likely to become better aligned when trabeculae are stretched, and this would contribute to the higher <P2> at longer SL.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: The effect of an increase in SL on the Ca2+ sensitivity of structural changes in the thin filaments reported by the cTnC probes is the same as that on force.
source: These results show that the effect of an increase in SL on the Ca2+ sensitivity of structural changes in the thin filaments reported by the cTnC probes is the same as that on force, but the higher maximum active force at longer SL is not accompanied by greater activation of the thin filament at maximum calcium activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The higher maximum active force at longer SL is not accompanied by greater activation of the thin filament at maximum calcium activation.
source: These results show that the effect of an increase in SL on the Ca2+ sensitivity of structural changes in the thin filaments reported by the cTnC probes is the same as that on force, but the higher maximum active force at longer SL is not accompanied by greater activation of the thin filament at maximum calcium activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The thin filament may already be fully activated at pCa 4.5 in control conditions at short SL.
source: These results suggest that the thin filament may already be fully activated at pCa 4.5 in control conditions at short SL, and that the length-dependent increase in maximum active force is determined by processes downstream of thin filament activation in the signalling pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: The length-dependent increase in maximum active force is determined by processes downstream of thin filament activation in the signalling pathway.
source: These results suggest that the thin filament may already be fully activated at pCa 4.5 in control conditions at short SL, and that the length-dependent increase in maximum active force is determined by processes downstream of thin filament activation in the signalling pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: Force-generating myosin heads sensitise the thin filament to calcium.
source: It is generally thought that force-generating myosin heads sensitise the thin filament to calcium (Moss et al., 2004; Smith et al., 2009), and this led to the idea that LDA might be a consequence of the higher force or number of myosin heads attached to actin at longer SL.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In the presence of 25 μM blebbistatin, the active force was reduced to 1.5% ± 0.4% (n = 12) of the control value.
source: In the presence of 25 μM blebbistatin, the active force was reduced to 1.5% ± 0.4% (n = 12) of the control value.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results.

claim: Blebbistatin may inhibit active force generation by stabilising the OFF structure of the myosin thick filament in which the myosin heads are folded back on the surface of the thick filaments and unavailable for interacting with actin in the thin filaments.
source: It should be noted that blebbistatin may inhibit active force generation by stabilising the OFF structure of the myosin thick filament in which the myosin heads are folded back on the surface of the thick filaments and unavailable for interacting with actin in the thin filaments (Zhao et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The Ca2+-sensitivity and steepness of the cTnC C helix orientational changes were reduced after addition of blebbistatin at SL 1.9 μm.
source: The Ca2+-sensitivity and steepness of the cTnC C helix orientational changes were reduced after addition of blebbistatin at SL 1.9 μm (Figure 4a, short-dashed line; Table 2), and pCa50 decreased by ~0.08 pCa units (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Figure 4a, 4c, and Table 2.

claim: The change in <P2> associated with activation (from pCa 6.0 to 4.5; Δ<P2>) was ~16% smaller after addition of blebbistatin (p<0.05).
source: The change in <P2> associated with activation (from pCa 6.0 to 4.5; Δ<P2>) was ~16% smaller after addition of blebbistatin (p<0.05; Table 2), although the effect of blebbistatin at each of these pCa values was not significant at the 5% level.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Table 2.

claim: For the E-helix probe, <P2> increased significantly on addition of blebbistatin at both pCa 6 and pCa 4.5.
source: Similar results were obtained for the E-helix probe (Figure 4b), except that <P2> increased significantly on addition of blebbistatin at both pCa 6 and pCa 4.5 (Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Figure 4b and Table 2.

claim: The addition of blebbistatin reduced the steepness of the Ca2+ dependence for both the C and E helix orientations (nH).
source: The addition of blebbistatin also reduced the steepness of the Ca2+ dependence for both the C and E helix orientations (nH, Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Table 2.

claim: Either active force increases myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity or stabilising the OFF structure of the thick filament decreases the Ca2+ sensitivity.
source: Similar results were obtained previously (Sun et al., 2009; Robertson et al., 2015), indicating that either active force increases myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity or stabilising the OFF structure of the thick filament decreases the Ca2+ sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current results and cited previous work.

claim: Increasing SL from 1.9 to 2.3 μm after addition of blebbistatin increased pCa50 by ~0.08 pCa units for both the C and E helix probes.
source: Increasing SL from 1.9 to 2.3 μm after addition of blebbistatin increased pCa50 by ~0.08 pCa units for both the C and E helix probes (Figure 4c and d, Table 2), similar to the ca 0.11 pCa unit increase observed before the addition of blebbistatin (p>0.05, two-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Figures 4c, 4d, and Table 2.

claim: The decrease in <P2> for the C-helix probe associated with activation (Δ <P2>) was smaller at the longer SL in the presence of blebbistatin (p<0.05).
source: The decrease in <P2> for the C-helix probe associated with activation (Δ <P2>) was smaller at the longer SL in the presence of blebbistatin (p<0.05, Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Table 2.

claim: For the E helix probe, increasing SL changed <P2> over the whole range of [Ca2+] in a direction characteristic of lower activation, with no change in Δ<P2>.
source: For the E helix probe, on the other hand, increasing SL changed <P2> over the whole range of [Ca2+] in a direction characteristic of lower activation, with no change in Δ<P2> (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The length-dependent increase in the Ca2+-sensitivity of cTnC structural changes is retained after complete force inhibition and stabilisation of the OFF structure of the thick filament.
source: These results show that the length-dependent increase in the Ca2+-sensitivity of cTnC structural changes is retained after complete force inhibition and stabilisation of the OFF structure of the thick filament.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The SL seems to directly modulate thin filament activation.
source: Thus, the SL seems to directly modulate thin filament activation, and the higher force/number of force-generating myosin heads at longer SL is NOT the main cause of higher Ca2+ sensitivity in LDA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The higher force/number of force-generating myosin heads at longer SL is NOT the main cause of higher Ca2+ sensitivity in LDA.
source: Thus, the SL seems to directly modulate thin filament activation, and the higher force/number of force-generating myosin heads at longer SL is NOT the main cause of higher Ca2+ sensitivity in LDA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The orientation of the BSR-cRLC-BC probe has previously been shown to be sensitive to both the change in orientation of the myosin heads associated with force generation per se and to interventions like RLC phosphorylation that alter the regulatory or structural state of the thick filament.
source: The orientation of this probe has previously been shown to be sensitive to both the change in orientation of the myosin heads associated with force generation per se and to interventions like RLC phosphorylation that alter the regulatory or structural state of the thick filament (Kampourakis et al., 2014, 2015, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: <P2> for the BSR-cRLC-BC probe increased when the trabeculae were activated at SL 1.9 μm and was further increased by stretching to SL 2.3 μm.
source: <P2> for the BSR-cRLC-BC probe increased when the trabeculae were activated at SL 1.9 μm and was further increased by stretching to SL 2.3 μm (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: <P2> increases with SL at both low (pCa 6.6) and high Ca2+ (pCa 4.5), but the effect was larger at high Ca2+.
source: Although <P2> increases with SL at both low (pCa 6.6) and high Ca2+ (pCa 4.5), the effect was larger at high Ca2+ (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The higher active force at longer SL is associated with length-dependent changes in the orientation of the myosin heads.
source: These results suggest that the higher active force at longer SL is associated with length-dependent changes in the orientation of the myosin heads.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Due to the flexibility of the central linker between the D- and E-helices in cTnC, the conformation of the N-terminal domain of cTnC (NcTnC), the regulatory head of troponin, moves dynamically during activation.
source: It has been shown previously that, due to the flexibility of the central linker between the D- and E-helices in cTnC, the conformation of the N-terminal domain of cTnC (NcTnC), the regulatory head of troponin, moves dynamically during activation (Sevrieva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Binding of Ca2+ to NcTnC and its subsequent interaction with the switch region of cTnI initiate the removal of cTnI from its actin binding site by bending NcTnC towards the C-terminal domain of cTnC.
source: Binding of Ca2+ to NcTnC and its subsequent interaction with the switch region of cTnI initiate the removal of cTnI from its actin binding site by bending NcTnC towards the C-terminal domain of cTnC (Takeda et al., 2003; Sevrieva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The C helix probe is likely to be much more sensitive to NcTnC re-orientation than to opening.
source: Considering that the opening of NcTnC due to Ca2+ binding and interaction with cTnI switch region is relatively small (Dong et al., 1999; Li et al., 1999), the C helix probe is likely to be much more sensitive to NcTnC re-orientation than to opening.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited previous work.

claim: The present results do not exclude the possibility that SL affects the opening of the NcTnC during cardiac muscle activation.
source: Thus, the present results do not exclude the possibility that SL affects the opening of the NcTnC during cardiac muscle activation (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study.

claim: The E-helix probe (BR-cTnC-E) in the IT arm of troponin is less likely to involve multi-domain conformational changes since the IT arm acts as a scaffold holding NcTnC and the actin binding regions of cTnI in a fixed orientation on the thin filament.
source: The E-helix probe (BR-cTnC-E) in the IT arm of troponin, on the other hand, is less likely to involve such multi-domain conformational changes since the IT arm acts as a scaffold holding NcTnC and the actin binding regions of cTnI in a fixed orientation on the thin filament (Sevrieva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited previous work.

claim: Increasing SL induced a change in the orientation of both cTnC probes in the direction associated with lower activation.
source: Increasing SL induced a change in the orientation of both cTnC probes in the direction associated with lower activation (Figure 2c and d).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the discussion and shown in Figures 2c and 2d.

claim: The SL-dependent change in the orientation of the E helix probe in the IT arm of troponin occurred over the whole range of [Ca2+], independent of the presence of force generating myosin heads.
source: In particular, the SL-dependent change in the orientation of the E helix probe in the IT arm of troponin occurred over the whole range of [Ca2+], independent of the presence of force generating myosin heads (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the discussion and shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The changes in troponin structure induced by increased SL are distinct from those induced by Ca2+ activation or force generation.
source: These results show that the changes in troponin structure induced by increased SL are distinct from those induced by Ca2+ activation or force generation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Increasing SL induces changes in troponin conformation in relaxed cardiac muscle cells.
source: A recent study by time-resolved small-angle X-ray diffraction also showed that increasing SL induces changes in troponin conformation in relaxed cardiac muscle cells (Ait-Mou et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: FRET measurements showed that the conformation of the switch region of cTnI relative to cTnC is also sensitive to SL in relaxed cardiac muscle.
source: In addition, FRET measurements showed that the conformation of the switch region of cTnI relative to cTnC is also sensitive to SL in relaxed cardiac muscle (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The SL-dependent changes in troponin structure could be related to the increased passive force at long SL.
source: These SL-dependent changes in troponin structure could be related to the increased passive force at long SL (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: In cardiac muscle cells, the passive force is attributed to the giant protein titin, which runs from the Z-disc to the M-line.
source: In cardiac muscle cells, the passive force is attributed to the giant protein titin, which runs from the Z-disc to the M-line (Labeit and Kolmerer, 1995; Granzier and Labeit, 2004; Patel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Titin-based passive force plays an important role in LDA.
source: Titin-based passive force plays an important role in LDA (Cazorla et al., 2001; Fukuda et al., 2001, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The length-dependent passive force is reduced in cardiac muscle from transgenic rats that express a giant splice isoform of titin.
source: The length-dependent passive force is reduced in cardiac muscle from transgenic rats that express a giant splice isoform of titin, and the length-dependent change in the X-ray troponin reflection is also reduced in these muscle cells (Ait-Mou et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Length-dependent changes in the structure of the thin filament of cardiac muscle can be one of the mechanisms underlying LDA, and hence the Frank-Starling law of the heart.
source: The combination of the present results with those of the X-ray and FRET studies mentioned above suggests that length-dependent changes in the structure of the thin filament of cardiac muscle can be one of the mechanisms underlying LDA, and hence the Frank-Starling law of the heart.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current results and cited previous work.

claim: The increase in maximum active force in LDA is likely to be determined by processes downstream of thin filament activation in the signalling pathway.
source: As discussed above, the increase in maximum active force in LDA is likely to be determined by processes downstream of thin filament activation in the signalling pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: <P2> for the BSR-cRLC-BC probe increased during Ca2+ activation and increased even further when SL was increased.
source: The present results have shown that <P2> for the BSR-cRLC-BC probe increased during Ca2+ activation and increased even further when SL was increased (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the discussion and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The length-dependent increase of isometric force in cardiac muscle is due to the change in the number of force-generating myosin heads.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that the length-dependent increase of isometric force in cardiac muscle is due to the change in the number of force-generating myosin heads (Caremani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The higher active force at longer SL is associated with a more ON state of the thick filament.
source: Together, these results show that the higher active force at longer SL is associated with a more ON state of the thick filament.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current results and cited previous work.

claim: X-ray measurements on resting cardiac muscle showed a close correlation between the orientation of myosin heads before activation and enhanced force generation as SL increases.
source: X-ray measurements on resting cardiac muscle showed a close correlation between the orientation of myosin heads before activation and enhanced force generation as SL increases, further supporting the idea of a direct effect of SL on thick filament structure (Farman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In resting cardiac muscles from rats that express the mutant titin, the SL-dependent changes in the intensities of the myosin-based X-ray reflections were greatly reduced, suggesting that titin-based passive force mediates the effect on thick filament structure.
source: In resting cardiac muscles from rats that express the mutant titin described above, the SL-dependent changes in the intensities of the myosin-based X-ray reflections were greatly reduced, suggesting that titin-based passive force mediates the effect on thick filament structure (Ait-Mou et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: An increase in SL in cardiac muscle results in increases in both the myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity and the maximum Ca2+-activated force.
source: It has long been established that an increase in SL in cardiac muscle results in increases in both the myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity and the maximum Ca2+-activated force (Kentish et al., 1986; Dobesh et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Two distinct pathways are involved in LDA.
source: The present results provided evidence that two distinct pathways are involved in LDA.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Increasing SL exerts a direct effect on the structure of troponin in the thin filament, which is the main contributor to the length-dependent increase of myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity in LDA.
source: Increasing SL exerts a direct effect on the structure of troponin in the thin filament, which is the main contributor to the length-dependent increase of myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity in LDA.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: A structural change of myosin in thick filament is responsible for the increase of maximal force generation in LDA.
source: A structural change of myosin in thick filament is responsible for the increase of maximal force generation in LDA.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: cTnI plays an important role in the LDA of cardiac muscle.
source: It is well known that cTnI plays an important role in the LDA of cardiac muscle (Arteaga et al., 2000; Konhilas et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser23/Ser24 at the cardiac-specific N-terminal region of cTnI enhances the length-dependent increase in Ca2+ sensitivity while having no effect on the length-dependent increase in maximum force.
source: It has also been shown that phosphorylation of Ser23/Ser24 at its cardiac-specific N-terminal region enhances the length-dependent increase in Ca2+ sensitivity while having no effect on the length-dependent increase in maximum force (Wijnker et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The increase in Ca2+ sensitivity in LDA is mediated through a change in thin filament structure.
source: This is in support of our conclusion that the increase in Ca2+ sensitivity in LDA is mediated through a change in thin filament structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current results and cited previous work.

claim: The thin filament mediated length-dependent change in Ca2+ sensitivity may play an important role in the development of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy by missense mutations in the sarcomeric proteins.
source: The thin filament mediated length-dependent change in Ca2+ sensitivity may play an important role in the development of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy by missense mutations in the sarcomeric proteins (Sequeira et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The LDA occurs immediately after a length change and independently of the increase in the intracellular [Ca2+].
source: The LDA occurs immediately after a length change and independently of the increase in the intracellular [Ca2+] (Allen and Kurihara, 1982; Mateja and de Tombe, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The passive force originated by titin plays a critical role in the transduction of the length signal to contractile apparatus in cardiac LDA.
source: Recent evidence has suggested that the passive force originated by titin plays a critical role in the transduction of the length signal to contractile apparatus in cardiac LDA (Fukuda et al., 2001; Methawasin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Increasing SL increases the passive force of cardiac muscle by stretching the titin that links the thick filament to the Z-disk and also relays its mechanical strain to the thick filament.
source: Increasing SL increases the passive force of cardiac muscle by stretching the titin that links the thick filament to the Z-disk and also relays its mechanical strain to the thick filament (Linke, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A recent X-ray study on skeletal muscle showed a connection between increased thick filament stress and its transition to ON state.
source: A recent X-ray study on skeletal muscle showed a connection between increased thick filament stress and its transition to ON state (Linari et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: This mechano-sensing mechanism may also exist in cardiac muscle as the X-ray measurement of cardiac muscle has indicated a structural rearrangement within the thick filament associated with titin strain and LDA.
source: This mechano-sensing mechanism may also exist in cardiac muscle as the X-ray measurement of cardiac muscle has indicated a structural rearrangement within the thick filament associated with titin strain and LDA (Ait-Mou et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Increasing SL in cardiac muscle changes the structure of troponin in the thin filament.
source: The results presented here, together with the previous studies described above, also demonstrated that increasing SL in cardiac muscle changes the structure of troponin in the thin filament.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current results and cited previous work.

claim: This length-dependent change in troponin structure is correlated with the titin strain and is present in the absence of active force-generating myosin heads.
source: This length-dependent change in troponin structure is correlated with the titin strain and is present in the absence of active force-generating myosin heads.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current results and cited previous work.

claim: MyBP-C may be involved in interfilament signal transmission.
source: It is not known how either titin strain or the ON state of the thick filament can be transmitted to the thin filament, although MyBP-C may be involved in this interfilament signal transmission.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: MyBP-C is localised to the central region of each half-thick filament.
source: MyBP-C is localised to the central region of each half-thick filament (Bennett et al., 1986; Luther et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MyBP-C is bound to the thick filament via its C-terminal region.
source: It is bound to the thick filament via its C-terminal region (Flashman et al., 2004) and its N-terminal region can activate the thin filament to trigger force generation in the absence of Ca2+ (Herron et al., 2006; Kampourakis et al., 2014; Mun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The N-terminal region of MyBP-C can activate the thin filament to trigger force generation in the absence of Ca2+.
source: It is bound to the thick filament via its C-terminal region (Flashman et al., 2004) and its N-terminal region can activate the thin filament to trigger force generation in the absence of Ca2+ (Herron et al., 2006; Kampourakis et al., 2014; Mun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In the absence of MyBP-C, while the length-dependent increase in the maximum force generation is preserved, the length-dependent increase in Ca2+ sensitivity is blunted.
source: In the absence of MyBP-C, while the length-dependent increase in the maximum force generation is preserved, the length-dependent increase in Ca2+ sensitivity is blunted (Mamidi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: cMyBP-C is one of the key components in modulating cardiac contractility in a manner that depends on its phosphorylation state.
source: cMyBP-C is one of the key components in modulating cardiac contractility in a manner that depends on its phosphorylation state (Gautel et al., 1995; Kunst et al., 2000; Pfuhl and Gautel, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Phosphorylation of MyBP-C inhibits the interaction of its N-terminal region with the thin filament.
source: Phosphorylation of MyBP-C, which inhibits the interaction of its N-terminal region with the thin filament (Shaffer et al., 2009; Kampourakis et al., 2014), has been shown to modulate LDA in cardiac muscle (Kumar et al., 2015; Mamidi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Phosphorylation of MyBP-C has been shown to modulate LDA in cardiac muscle.
source: Phosphorylation of MyBP-C, which inhibits the interaction of its N-terminal region with the thin filament (Shaffer et al., 2009; Kampourakis et al., 2014), has been shown to modulate LDA in cardiac muscle (Kumar et al., 2015; Mamidi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MyBP-C is a strong candidate for transmitting the signal of titin strain generated by SL change from the thick to the thin filament.
source: Thus, MyBP-C is a strong candidate for transmitting the signal of titin strain generated by SL change from the thick to the thin filament.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the current results and cited previous work.

source: All animal procedures were in accordance with Schedule 1 of the UK Animal (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986.
evidence: This is a statement about the ethical compliance of the study.

source: Adult Wistar rats (200–250 g) were sacrificed by cervical dislocation.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Endogenous cTnC was exchanged by incubation of trabeculae in relaxing solution containing 25–30 μM BR-cTnC overnight at 4°C.
source: Endogenous cTnC was exchanged by incubation of trabeculae in relaxing solution containing 25–30 μM BR-cTnC overnight at 4°C.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The fraction of cTnC replaced by BR-TnC was about 80%.
source: The fraction of cTnC replaced by BR-TnC was about 80% (Sevrieva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods supported by a citation.

claim: BSR-cRLCs were exchanged into demembranated trabeculae by extraction in CDTA-rigor solution for 30 min followed by reconstitution with 40 mM BSR-cRLC in relaxing solution for 1 hr, replacing 30–50% of the endogenous cRLCs.
source: BSR-cRLCs were exchanged into demembranated trabeculae by extraction in CDTA-rigor solution (mM: 5 CDTA, 50 KCl, 40 Tris-HCl pH 8.4, 0.1% (v/v) Triton X-100) for 30 min followed by reconstitution with 40 mM BSR-cRLC in relaxing solution for 1 hr, replacing 30–50% of the endogenous cRLCs (Kampourakis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods supported by a citation.

claim: The steepness of the Ca2+-force relationships in the present study (nH = ~4) was less than that in a study where SL was kept constant during the contraction by adjusting overall muscle length.
source: The steepness of the Ca2+-force relationships in the present study (nH = ~4, Table 1) was less than that in a study where SL was kept constant during the contraction by adjusting overall muscle length (Dobesh et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current results with cited previous work.

claim: The end-compliance of trabecular preparations allows SL shortening during activation.
source: This is likely due to the end-compliance of trabecular preparations that allows SL shortening during activation (ter Keurs et al., 1980; Kentish et al., 1986).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited previous work.

claim: As the trabecula generates more force at higher concentrations of Ca2+, the central sarcomeres shorten more.
source: As the trabecula generates more force at higher concentrations of Ca2+, the central sarcomeres shorten more.
evidence: This is an inference about the experimental system.

claim: Both pCa50 and nH of the Ca2+-force relationship at a given SL were likely to be underestimated in fixed end conditions as in the present study.
source: Therefore, both pCa50 and nH of the Ca2+-force relationship at a given SL were likely to be underestimated in fixed end conditions as in the present study.
